Ligand preference model

Enter the decision codes from everyone in the class. The model learns what the class values in a route and a ligand from their decisions, and updates as each code comes in.

1 · The class’s decision codes

The brief everyone decided for:

Each job done in the ligand decisions app gives one code, carrying its ten decisions. Enter every code from the class. You can type several at once, separated by spaces. A second code for the same job replaces the first.

How the model learns your preferences

Giving a route a score out of 10 is hard; saying which you would rather use is easy. So each decision in the stage 1 app is a choice between two ligands, each by one of its routes: which would you rather make? Each records “A is preferred to B”.

The Bradley–Terry model (1952) turns such choices into a ranking. Each option gets a score, and the bigger the gap between two scores, the more likely the higher one is chosen: P(A preferred to B) = 1 / (1 + e−(score A − score B)).

Here a ligand’s score, by a given route, is a weighted sum of five criteria (steps, average step atom economy, starting materials on sale, worst hazard and SCScore, each put on a common scale). Training finds the weights that make the class’s actual choices as likely as possible, with a small penalty that keeps them modest when there are few decisions.

The decisions were chosen so the five criteria vary independently of each other, in every job and in any number of jobs from job 1 up, so the model can tell them apart. Most decisions are in two neighbouring jobs, and two (the anchors) are in every job, so the page can show how far the class agrees.

The weights show what the class valued, and they can score every route of every ligand, including ones nobody looked at. The same idea rates chess players (Elo) and trains the reward models that align chatbots with human preferences.

2 · Preference model

Training fits one weight per criterion so that, for as many of the class’s decisions as possible, the ligand chosen gets the higher score (a Bradley–Terry model). A small penalty keeps the weights modest when there are few decisions. It retrains itself whenever a code comes in.

3 · Ligand hierarchy

Every route of every ligand, scored with the learned weights: including the routes and ligands nobody compared. Each decision showed one route per ligand, so for some ligands the model’s favourite route is one the class never saw.

Routes proposed by AiZynthFinder 4.4 (Genheden et al., J. Cheminform. 2020, 12, 70) with its public USPTO template and filter models and its stock of commercially available compounds (from the ZINC database), precomputed for each ligand so the class does not wait for the search. Search settings: Monte Carlo tree search; USPTO template expansion model (42,554 templates); stock of 17.4 million commercially available compounds; at most 6 steps; 90 s per target. The target itself is removed from the stock so a synthesis is proposed even for commercially available ligands. Templates show reactants only: reagents, catalysts and solvents are not predicted, and step names are assigned from the bonds formed and broken. Atom economy counts the reactants only, so it is an upper bound; the criterion is the average over the route’s steps, so it does not simply fall with every extra step. For ten ligands the model proposes no route (eight ferrocenes, which the templates do not cover, tri-tert-butylphosphine and 4,4′-di-tert-butyl-2,2′-bipyridine): they have only their published synthesis, entered by hand, and in the decisions app they are compared by that route. SCScore: Coley et al., J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2018, 58, 252, a neural network trained on 12 million published reactions to score products above their reactants; computed with the authors' published weights; not trained on ferrocenes, so not shown for them (†) and treated by the model as average. Worst hazard: the most severe hazard statement of any substance in the route (reactants, intermediates and the ligand), in five levels. Level 5: H340, H350, H360, H300, H310, H330, H420. Level 4: H314. Level 3: H341, H351, H361, H370, H372, H301, H311, H331, H400, H410, H411. Level 2: H334, H318, H412, H413 and all physical hazards (H2xx). Level 1: H304, H371, H373, H302, H312, H332, H336, H315, H317, H319, H335. In the model it is the level plus a tenth for each substance at that level (up to nine), so more substances at the same level count as slightly worse. Substances with no safety data are left out, and shown by the grey “?” diamond beside the GHS symbols, which are assigned from the same H-codes with the label precedence rules of the CLP Regulation. Pictogram artwork: UNECE GHS pictograms.
